battle:丹阳之战.cmd: Wei Zhang and Chuli Ji vs. Qu Gai
battle:丹阳之战.mod: Dan River valley between Xichuan, Henan and Shangnan, Shaanxi
battle:丹阳之战.note: Deceived by Zhang Yi's promise of "six hundred li of Shang and Wu", King Huai of Chu attacked Qin in anger and was routed at Danyang; eighty thousand were beheaded and Qu Gai captured, and Qin took six hundred li of Chu's Hanzhong and set up Hanzhong Commandery.

battle:伊阙之战.note: Bai Qi defeated a larger army, beheading two hundred and forty thousand, capturing the Wei general Gongsun Xi and taking five towns. This battle made Bai Qi's name.

battle:修鱼之战.note: In 318 BC Gongsun Yan organised a vertical alliance of five states against Qin; the alliance was defeated at Hangu Pass; the next year the Qin army pursued and took eighty-two thousand heads at Xiuyu.
battle:修鱼之战.sides: Qin defeated Han, Zhao and Wei

battle:北击匈奴.note: After touring the northern frontier, the First Emperor sent Meng Tian with three hundred thousand men against the Xiongnu; he took all Henandi (south of the Hetao bend), and Touman Chanyu moved north. The next year Jiuyuan Commandery was set up and forty-four counties were established from Yuzhong east along the He, "using the river as a barrier".

battle:华阳之战.note: Wei and Zhao attacked Huayang in Han; Bai Qi rushed to its relief, beheaded a hundred and thirty thousand and drowned twenty thousand Zhao troops in the He. Wei ceded Nanyang to make peace.

battle:南征百越.cmd: Tu Sui, then Ren Xiao and Zhao Tuo vs. Yixusong, lord of the Xi'ou
battle:南征百越.note: The First Emperor sent five hundred thousand men south along five routes against the Hundred Yue. The Qin army killed Yixusong, lord of the Xi'ou, but the Yue fled into the forests, raided the Qin troops at night and killed their commander Tu Sui; "corpses lay and blood flowed, several hundred thousand" (Huainanzi, "Renjian xun"). Only after cutting the Lingqu Canal to bring up supplies did Qin advance again and finally pacify Lingnan.
battle:南征百越.old: Southern campaign against the Hundred Yue
battle:南征百越.sides: Qin defeated the Hundred Yue (after early defeats)

battle:即墨之战.note: King Hui of Yan fell for a ruse to sow discord and replaced Yue Yi with Qi Jie. Tian Dan raided the Yan camp at night with his "fire-ox formation", the Yan army collapsed, and Qi recovered all of its seventy-odd towns.

battle:取高阙·北假.mod: Urad Front Banner – Lang Mountains, Inner Mongolia
battle:取高阙·北假.note: Meng Tian crossed the He and took Gaoque, the Yang Mountains and Beijia, building watchtowers and stockades to drive out the Rong, and moved banished convicts there to fill the new counties.

battle:垂沙之战.note: The three allied armies crossed the Ci River by night and crushed Chu; Tang Mei was killed, and Chu lost its land north of Wan and She. Zhuang Qiao rose in revolt amid the turmoil, and "Chu split into three or four".
battle:垂沙之战.sides: Qi, Han and Wei defeated Chu

battle:城父之战.cmd: Xiang Yan vs. Li Xin and Meng Tian
battle:城父之战.note: Li Xin invaded Chu with two hundred thousand men; Xiang Yan followed him for three days and three nights without stopping to camp, and crushed him at Chengfu; the Qin army fled.

battle:大梁之战.note: Wang Ben flooded Daliang with water from the Yellow River and the Honggou Canal; after three months the walls gave way, Jia, king of Wei, surrendered, and Wei fell.

battle:宜阳之战.note: King Wu of Qin wanted "a road for chariots through Sanchuan, to peer at the house of Zhou"; Gan Mao besieged Yiyang for five months, took it and beheaded sixty thousand. This opened Qin's gateway east into the Central Plains.

battle:平定岭南.note: Ren Xiao and Zhao Tuo led the army that pacified Lingnan; the Nanhai, Guilin and Xiang commanderies were set up and five hundred thousand convicts from the Central Plains were moved there as garrison. When Ren Xiao died at the end of Qin, Zhao Tuo took Lingnan for himself and founded the kingdom of Nanyue.

battle:易水之战.note: After Jing Ke's failed attempt on the king of Qin, Qin invaded Yan in force and defeated the allied Yan and Dai armies west of the Yi River; the next year (226 BC) it took Ji.

battle:晋阳之战.cmd: Viscount Xiang of Zhao vs. Zhi Yao
battle:晋阳之战.note: Zhi Yao, Earl of Zhi, diverted the Jin River to flood Jinyang until "only three boards' height of the wall stayed above water"; Viscount Xiang of Zhao sent Zhang Mengtan to win over Han and Wei, and the three lineages counterattacked, destroyed the Zhi lineage and divided their land. This laid the foundation for the partition of Jin, and historians often take it as one of the markers of the start of the Warring States.
battle:晋阳之战.sides: Zhao, Han and Wei defeated the Zhi lineage

battle:李牧破匈奴.mod: N of the Datong (Shanxi) – Zhangjiakou (Hebei) line
battle:李牧破匈奴.note: Guarding Dai and Yanmen, Li Mu feigned weakness to lure the enemy, crushed more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen in a single battle, destroyed the Chanlan, broke the Donghu and received the surrender of the Linhu; for more than ten years afterwards the Xiongnu dared not approach Zhao's frontier.

battle:桂陵之战.cmd: Tian Ji and Sun Bin vs. Pang Juan
battle:桂陵之战.mod: NW of Changyuan, Henan (one view: Heze, Shandong)
battle:桂陵之战.note: Wei besieged Handan, the Zhao capital; Qi followed Sun Bin's plan to "besiege Wei to rescue Zhao", marched straight on Daliang, and crushed the Wei army at Guiling as it hurried back to relieve its capital.

battle:楚围雍氏（一）.note: In the same year as the Battle of Danyang, the Chu general Jing Cui marched north and besieged Yongshi in Han, just as King Xuanhui of Han died. Qin, while routing Chu at Danyang, sent Chuli Ji to help Han, and Chu lifted the siege and withdrew. Bamboo Annals: "Jing Cui of Chu besieged Yongshi; King Xuan of Han died; Qin helped Han and together they defeated Qu Gai of Chu."

battle:楚围雍氏（三）.note: After the death of Ying, crown prince of Han, Prince Jiu contended for the succession with Prince Jishi, a hostage in Chu. Chu, wanting to install Jishi, besieged Yongshi with its army; Han appealed to Qin, Chu finally lifted the siege and withdrew, and Prince Jiu became crown prince: the later King Xi of Han (the Han chapter of the Shiji). Bamboo Annals (quoted in the Jijie commentary to the Han chapter): "Chu entered Yongshi; the men of Chu were defeated."

battle:楚围雍氏（二）.cmd: King Huai of Chu vs. Gongzhong Chi
battle:楚围雍氏（二）.note: Resenting Han's failure to help at Danyang, King Huai of Chu besieged Yongshi for five months. Han sent Gongzhong Chi and then Shang Jin to Qin for help; Queen Dowager Xuan, a native of Chu, at first would not send troops, but Gan Mao persuaded King Zhao of Qin that "if Chu and Han become one, an attack on Qin will take shape"; the Qin army came out through the Xiao Mountains, and the Chu troops left.

battle:楚威王败越.cmd: King Wei of Chu vs. Wujiang, king of Yue
battle:楚威王败越.mod: between the Yangtze and the Huai (approx.)
battle:楚威王败越.note: According to the Yue chapter of the Shiji, Wujiang, king of Yue, marched north against Qi; an envoy from Qi persuaded him to turn against Chu instead, and King Wei of Chu routed Yue and also "crushed Qi at Xuzhou in the north" (333 BC). Tradition takes this as the year Yue fell; but in 312 BC the king of Yue still sent envoys to present boats to Wei, so it is now widely held that in this battle Chu took only part of Yue's lands between the Yangtze and the Huai, and that Yue did not fall.
battle:楚威王败越.old: King Wei of Chu defeats Yue

battle:楚灭越.cmd: King Huai of Chu and Shao Hua vs. Wujiang, king of Yue
battle:楚灭越.note: King Huai of Chu sent Shao Hua into Yue to sow discord: "within, he stirred up the troubles of Zhangyi, and Yue fell into chaos; therefore Chu closed Limen in the south and made Jiangdong a commandery" (Fan Yuan's words, biography of Gan Mao in the Shiji). Chu attacked Yue in the turmoil, killed Wujiang, king of Yue, took all the old lands of Wu up to the Zhe River, and set up Jiangdong Commandery. Yue broke apart, and its princes, "some becoming kings and some lords", submitted and paid court to Chu.

battle:河外之战.note: Lord Xinling returned to Wei, led the forces of five states to crush Meng Ao at Hewai, and pursued him to Hangu Pass; the Qin army dared not come out.
battle:河外之战.sides: Wei, Zhao, Han, Chu and Yan defeated Qin

battle:济西之战.mod: W of the Ji River, between Liaocheng and Gaotang, Shandong
battle:济西之战.note: The five allied armies crushed the Qi army west of the Ji River, and Yue Yi drove deep into Qi with the Yan army, taking seventy-odd Qi towns in half a year; King Min of Qi fled to Ju and was killed by the Chu general Nao Chi.
battle:济西之战.sides: Yan, Qin, Han, Zhao and Wei defeated Qi

battle:番吾之战.note: Qin attacked Zhao along two routes; Li Mu defeated the Qin army again at Powu and held off Han and Wei in the south.

battle:石门之战.note: Qin took sixty thousand heads, and King Xian of Zhou sent Duke Xian of Qin embroidered ceremonial robes in congratulation. It marked the point at which Qin turned from defence to attack.

battle:秦开却东胡.note: Qin Kai had once been a hostage among the Donghu and knew them well; back in Yan he routed the Donghu, who fell back more than a thousand li; Yan set up five commanderies and built a long wall from Zaoyang to Xiangping.
battle:秦开却东胡.old: Qin Kai drives back the Donghu

battle:秦灭巴蜀.cmd: Sima Cuo and Zhang Yi vs. the king of Shu
battle:秦灭巴蜀.note: Shu attacked Ju; the Marquis of Ju fled to Ba, and Ba and Ju appealed to Qin for help. King Huiwen of Qin followed Sima Cuo's advice and attacked Shu by the Jinniu (Shiniu) Road; the king of Shu was defeated at Jiameng and died at Wuyang, and Qin destroyed Shu and "went on to take Ju and Ba". As Sima Cuo had argued, "its land is enough to enlarge the state, its wealth enough to enrich the people".
battle:秦灭巴蜀.old: Qin conquest of Ba and Shu
battle:秦灭巴蜀.sides: Qin defeated Shu, Ju and Ba

battle:秦破赵.cmd: Wang Jian and Yang Duanhe vs. Zhao Cong and Yan Ju
battle:秦破赵.note: Qin sowed discord and Qian, king of Zhao, had Li Mu killed; Wang Jian came out through the Jingxing Pass and Yang Duanhe attacked Handan, crushing the Zhao army and capturing him.

battle:肥之战.note: Li Mu crushed the Qin army at Fei; Huan Yi fled (one view: was killed), and Li Mu was made Lord Wu'an.

battle:蓝田之战.note: King Huai of Chu threw the state's entire army deep into Qin as far as Lantian and was defeated again; Han and Wei seized the chance to raid Chu as far south as Deng, forcing Chu to withdraw, gravely weakened.

battle:蕞之战.note: The last vertical alliance of the states east of the mountains, led by the Zhao general Pang Nuan, reached Zui, not far from Xianyang, but was finally defeated and turned back. As a result Chu moved its capital to Shouchun.
battle:蕞之战.sides: Qin defeated Zhao, Chu, Wei, Yan and Han

battle:蕲南之战.cmd: Wang Jian and Meng Wu vs. Xiang Yan
battle:蕲南之战.note: Wang Jian, with six hundred thousand men, stayed behind his ramparts and would not fight; when the Chu army withdrew east he pursued it and crushed it at Qinan; Xiang Yan died (one view: killed himself), and Fuchu, king of Chu, was captured.

battle:襄陵之战.note: Zhao Yang, pillar of state of Chu, defeated Wei at Xiangling and took eight towns. Chen Zhen, with the parable of "drawing legs on a snake", persuaded Zhao Yang to quit while he was ahead and call off an attack on Qi.

battle:赵灭中山.note: King Wuling of Zhao attacked Zhongshan year after year with troops trained in nomad dress and mounted archery, destroyed it in 296 BC and moved its king to Fushi. Zhao's Dai region and Handan were now joined into one.

battle:邯郸之战.cmd: Wang Ling and Wang He vs. Lord Pingyuan, Lord Xinling and Lord Chunshen
battle:邯郸之战.note: Following up its victory at Changping, Qin besieged Handan for nearly three years; Lord Pingyuan went to Chu for help, where Mao Sui put himself forward and sealed the vertical alliance; Lord Xinling of Wei stole the tally to rescue Zhao, and the Qin army was routed.
battle:邯郸之战.sides: Zhao, Wei and Chu defeated Qin

battle:鄢郢之战.note: Bai Qi diverted the waters of a long valley in the western hills to flood the city of Yan, drowning hundreds of thousands of Chu soldiers and civilians; the next year he took Ying and burned Yiling (the tombs of the Chu kings); Chu moved its capital to Chen, and Qin set up Nan Commandery.

battle:长平之战.cmd: Bai Qi and Wang He vs. Lian Po, then Zhao Kuo
battle:长平之战.note: Han's Shangdang surrendered its seventeen towns to Zhao, setting off a decisive war between Qin and Zhao. Zhao replaced Lian Po with Zhao Kuo, who attacked, was surrounded for forty-six days and was killed; more than four hundred thousand surrendered troops were buried alive. After this none of the six states could stand up to Qin alone.

battle:阏与之战.mod: W of Heshun, Shanxi (one view: Qin County)
battle:阏与之战.note: Holding that "when two meet on a narrow road, the braver wins", Zhao She seized the northern hill and crushed the Qin army, and was made Lord Mafu. Qin then turned to Fan Ju's policy of "ally with the distant, attack the near".

battle:阴晋之战.note: According to the Wuzi, Wu Qi defeated a Qin host of five hundred thousand with fifty thousand Wei troops (the numbers may be exaggerated). Wei held Hexi for several decades, and Qin "could not come out to the east".

battle:雕阴之战.note: Qin killed eighty thousand Wei troops, and Wei was forced to hand over all of Hexi; in 328 BC it also ceded the fifteen counties of Shang Commandery, giving Qin complete control west of the Yellow River.

battle:马陵之战.cmd: Tian Ji and Sun Bin vs. Pang Juan and Crown Prince Shen
battle:马陵之战.mod: around Fan County, Henan – Shen County, Shandong (one view: Tancheng, Shandong)
battle:马陵之战.note: Sun Bin feigned weakness by "reducing the cooking fires" to lure the enemy on, and hid ten thousand crossbowmen along the Maling road; Pang Juan, outwitted, cut his own throat, and Shen, crown prince of Wei, was captured. Wei's hegemony collapsed as a result.

battle:齐灭宋.note: Yan, ruler of Song, was a tyrant known as "the Jie of Song"; King Min of Qi destroyed Song, alarming the other lords, and this became the direct trigger of the five-state attack on Qi.

capital:中牟.note: Marquis Xian of Zhao moved the capital to Zhongmou. Its location is much debated; one view puts it between modern Hebi and Tangyin in Henan.

capital:临淄.note: Capital of Qi, said to have seventy thousand households: "hubs knock against hubs, shoulders rub against shoulders; joined lapels make a curtain, raised sleeves make an awning" (Su Qin). The Jixia Academy lay outside its Ji Gate. Usually counted among Qi's "Five Capitals" (Linzi, Pinglu, Gaotang, Jimo, Ju), each with a standing army, the "troops of the Five Capitals".

capital:代.note: Originally the state of Dai, destroyed by Viscount Xiang of Zhao (457 BC). In 228 BC Prince Jia of Zhao fled to Dai and styled himself king; he was captured by Wang Ben in 222 BC.

capital:会稽.note: Early capital of Yue, where Goujian "slept on brushwood and tasted gall". After Chu destroyed Yue (c. 306 BC) the Yue chieftains held out south of the Zhe River; in 222 BC Wang Jian received the surrender of the lords of Yue and set up Kuaiji Commandery here.

capital:吴.note: Capital of the Spring and Autumn state of Wu. In 379 BC Yi, king of Yue, moved his capital here from Langya; after Chu destroyed Yue around 306 BC it passed to Chu as part of Jiangdong Commandery; in 248 BC Lord Chunshen was re-enfeoffed in Jiangdong and lived in the ruins of old Wu.

capital:咸阳.note: Built under Shang Yang's direction; Duke Xiao of Qin moved the capital here in 350 BC. The Wei River ran through the city, and after unification it was the capital of the whole realm.

capital:商丘.note: Capital of Song, home of the descendants of the Shang. Taken by King Min of Qi in 286 BC.

capital:大梁.note: King Hui of Wei moved the capital here, so Wei came to be called "Liang"; Mencius's audience with King Hui of Liang took place here. Taken in 225 BC when the Qin army flooded the city.

capital:安邑.note: Wei's first capital, near the salt revenues of Lake Xie; Li Kui's reforms took place here. The capital moved to Daliang in 361 BC (or 364 BC).

capital:宜阳.note: For a time the capital of Viscount Wu of Han; a key town on Han's western border, "a county in name, a commandery in fact". Taken by the Qin general Gan Mao in 307 BC.

capital:寿春.note: The last capital of Chu, also called "Ying". Taken by Qin in 223 BC, when Fuchu, king of Chu, was captured.

capital:巨阳.note: Where King Kaolie of Chu moved the capital; its exact location is still unsettled.

capital:巩.note: Capital of the lord of East Zhou. In 249 BC the Qin chancellor Lü Buwei destroyed East Zhou.

capital:平阳.note: Where the Han lineage first lived.

capital:成都.note: Capital of the Kaiming lineage of Shu. After the Qin conquest Zhang Yi and Zhang Ruo built the walls of Chengdu.

capital:新郑.note: Originally the capital of the state of Zheng; Marquis Ai of Han moved the capital here after destroying Zheng in 375 BC. Shen Buhai and Han Fei both worked here.

capital:晋阳.note: Built by Viscount Jian of Zhao; in 453 BC the Earl of Zhi flooded Jinyang, and the three lineages counterattacked and destroyed the Zhi lineage.

capital:曲阜.note: Capital of Lu and home town of Confucius. Lu was destroyed by Chu in 256 BC.

capital:栎阳.note: Duke Xian of Qin moved east here to contend for Hexi; Shang Yang's first reforms were proclaimed here, and "moving the log to establish trust" took place at Yueyang.

capital:武阳.mod: Yi County, Hebei (Lower Capital of Yan)
capital:武阳.note: Lower Capital of Yan, built around the reign of King Zhao; about 8 km from east to west, one of the largest city sites of the Warring States.

capital:濮阳.note: Diqiu, capital of Wey. Taken by Qin in 241 BC and made Dong Commandery.

capital:灵寿.note: Capital of Zhongshan after its restoration; the city site and the tomb of King Cuo of Zhongshan have both been excavated.

capital:王城.note: The royal city of Eastern Zhou; after Zhou split it was the seat of the lord of West Zhou, and King Nan of Zhou also lodged here. West Zhou was destroyed by Qin in 256 BC.

capital:琅琊.note: After destroying Wu, Goujian moved north here to contend for hegemony in the Central Plains (according to the Bamboo Annals and other sources); Yue later moved back south to Wu.

capital:葭萌.note: Capital of Ju, the town enfeoffed to the Marquis of Ju, younger brother of the king of Shu, commanding the Jinniu Road. After destroying Ju, Qin set up Jiameng County; in the Three Kingdoms Shu-Han renamed it Hanshou.

capital:蓟.note: Upper Capital of Yan. Taken by the Qin general Wang Jian in 226 BC.

capital:襄平.note: Seat of Yan's Liaodong Commandery. In 226 BC Xi, king of Yan, abandoned Ji and fell back here; he was captured by Wang Ben in 222 BC.

capital:邯郸.note: Marquis Jing of Zhao moved the capital here. A great northern centre of iron-working and trade; the idiom "learning to walk in Handan" comes from here.

capital:郢.note: Capital of Chu for more than four hundred years (the Jinancheng ruins). In 278 BC Bai Qi took Ying and burned the tombs of the Chu kings at Yiling.

capital:野王.note: Qin moved Jue, lord of Wey, here, and Wey lingered on as a Qin dependency until 209 BC.

capital:阆中.note: One of the later capitals of Ba.

capital:阳翟.note: Marquis Jing of Han moved the capital here. Lü Buwei began as a "great merchant of Yangzhai".

capital:陈.note: Originally the capital of the state of Chen; King Qingxiang of Chu moved east here after losing Ying, and it was called "Ying-Chen".

capital:雍.note: Capital of Qin for nearly three hundred years (677–383 BC) and site of Great Tomb No. 1 of the Qin dukes; after the capital moved it remained the centre of the ancestral temples and sacrifices.

capital:顾.note: First capital of Duke Wu of Zhongshan.

city:上党.note: Han's Shangdang Commandery (seat around Zhangzi). In 262 BC its governor Feng Ting surrendered its seventeen towns to Zhao, setting off the Battle of Changping.

city:上蔡.note: Former capital of the state of Cai and a key northern town of Chu; home town of Li Si.

city:东郡.note: In 242 BC Qin took Suanzao and nineteen other Wei towns and set up Dong Commandery, a wedge driven between Qi, Wei and Zhao that cut the north–south links of the vertical alliance east of the mountains.

city:九原.note: The limit of King Wuling of Zhao's conquests; under Qin, Jiuyuan Commandery and the northern end of the Qin Straight Road.

city:云中.note: Seat of the Yunzhong Commandery set up by King Wuling of Zhao.

city:南郑.note: Centre of the Hanzhong basin, fought over repeatedly by Qin and Shu: in 451 BC Qin "walled Nanzheng"; in 441 BC "Nanzheng rebelled"; in 387 BC, by one account Qin "attacked Shu and took Nanzheng" (Basic Annals of Qin in the Shiji), by another "Shu took our Nanzheng" (Table of the Six States in the Shiji). In the mid Warring States it belonged to Shu; it passed to Qin in 316 BC and later became the seat of Qin's Hanzhong Commandery.

city:即墨.note: With Ju, one of the only two Qi towns that held out after Yue Yi crushed Qi; Tian Dan restored the state from here. One of Qi's "Five Capitals".

city:商.note: Duke Xiao of Qin enfeoffed Shang Yang with the fifteen towns of Shang and Wu, styling him Lord Shang. Zhang Yi once deceived Chu with "six hundred li of the land of Shang and Wu".

city:宛.note: Centre of the Nanyang basin and a major iron-working town of Chu: "the steel spears of Wan sting like bees and scorpions". Qin set up Nanyang Commandery in 272 BC.

city:平原.note: Key place in northwestern Qi. The title of Lord Pingyuan, Zhao Sheng of Zhao, comes from the area of Dongwucheng in Zhao; it is close to this place name (but this was not his fief).

city:平陆.note: One of Qi's "Five Capitals", the southwestern gateway guarding against Lu, Song and Wei. Mencius came to Pinglu and told its grandee Kong Juxin, "in years of disaster and famine, the old and weak among your people are tossed into the ditches" (Mencius, "Gongsun Chou II").

city:广陵.note: In the 10th year of King Huai of Chu (319 BC) Guangling was walled. At that time the Yangtze entered the sea near here, and the river was very wide.

city:彭城.note: Key town in eastern Song (one view: Song moved its capital here late in its history); passed to Chu after Song fell.

city:武遂.mod: SE of Yuanqu, Shanxi (one view: near Linfen)
city:武遂.note: A Han town on the north bank of the Yellow River, facing Yiyang across the river; "two hundred li of Wusui land" refers to this land north of the river. Qin and Han fought over it repeatedly: in 307 BC, after taking Yiyang, Qin "crossed the river and walled Wusui"; in 306 BC Gan Mao urged its return to Han; in 303 BC Qin took it again; in 296 BC, after Qi, Han and Wei broke through Hangu, Qin "gave Han Hewai and Wusui" to make peace; in 290 BC Han ceded "two hundred li of Wusui land" to Qin (Basic Annals of Qin, Han chapter and biography of Gan Mao in the Shiji). There are two views of its location: here it is placed SE of Yuanqu following "crossed the river and walled Wusui"; the Chu chapter of the Shiji says Han's "former kings' tombs are at Pingyang, and Qin's Wusui is seventy li from them", and Pingyang lies SW of modern Linfen, so one view puts Wusui near Linfen. There was also a Yan town called Wusui (W of modern Xushui, Hebei), taken by the Zhao general Li Mu in 243 BC; it is not the same place.

city:洛阳.note: "The centre of the realm", seat of the Zhou royal domain; Su Qin was a native of Luoyang.

city:狄道.note: Seat of Qin's Longxi Commandery, where the Long Wall of King Zhao of Qin began in the west.

city:肤施.note: Seat of Qin's Shang Commandery; after destroying Zhongshan, Zhao moved the king of Zhongshan to Fushi.

city:荥阳.note: Where the He and the Ji meet, site of the Ao Granary and start of the Honggou Canal; the hub of water and land transport in the Central Plains.

city:莒.note: Where King Min of Qi fled; King Xiang of Qi took the throne at Ju and held it for five years. One of Qi's "Five Capitals", guarding the south against Chu.

city:薛.note: Fief of Lord Mengchang, Tian Wen, who kept several thousand retainers, among them the men "who crowed like cocks and stole like dogs".

city:邺.note: Under Marquis Wen of Wei, Ximen Bao as magistrate of Ye ended the custom of "brides for the River Lord" and dug twelve canals from the Zhang River, making Ye prosperous. For most of the Warring States it belonged to Wei; in 239 BC Wei ceded Ye to Zhao, and in 236 BC Wang Jian and other Qin generals attacked Zhao and took Ye.

city:鄢.note: Secondary capital of Chu (Yan-Ying). In 279 BC Bai Qi flooded the city.

city:金陵.note: By tradition King Wei of Chu set up the town of Jinling after defeating Yue (c. 333 BC; the account comes from Song-dynasty gazetteers and its reliability is doubtful); this is the origin of Nanjing's name "Jinling".

city:长沙.note: Key town on Chu's southern frontier, where the Chu silk manuscript and many other Chu artefacts have been found; Qin set up Changsha Commandery.

city:阿.note: Key town in western Qi; Sun Bin was born "between E and Juan". King Wei of Qi "boiled the grandee of E" here; one view counts it among Qi's "Five Capitals" (in place of Linzi).

city:陶.note: "The centre of the realm", with roads to every state; Fan Li settled here, grew rich in trade and was called Lord Zhu of Tao. The Qin chancellor Wei Ran was enfeoffed here.

city:雍氏.note: A Han town about twenty-five li NE of the old capital Yangzhai, on the road by which Chu armies came north out of Fangcheng to threaten the Han capital Xinzheng. Chu besieged Yongshi three times: in 312 BC the Chu general Jing Cui besieged it and Qin helped Han defeat Chu (Bamboo Annals; Basic Annals of Qin in the Shiji); in 307 BC (or 306 BC) King Huai of Chu, resenting Han's failure to help at Danyang, besieged Yongshi for five months, Gan Mao persuaded Qin to send troops to save Han, and the Chu troops left (biography of Gan Mao in the Shiji; second Han section of the Zhanguo ce); in 300 BC, after Ying, crown prince of Han, died and Prince Jiu and Prince Jishi contended for the succession, Chu besieged Yongshi and finally lifted the siege and withdrew (Han chapter of the Shiji).

city:高唐.note: One of Qi's "Five Capitals", a key northwestern town on the ancient Yellow River guarding against Zhao. King Wei of Qi: "I have a minister called Panzi; I have him guard Gaotang, and the men of Zhao dare not come east to fish in the He."

culture:中山王墓.note: The tomb of King Cuo of Zhongshan yielded a bronze square table with four dragons and four phoenixes inlaid with gold and silver, the bronze "Zhaoyu tu" plate (one of the earliest architectural plans) and the "Three Vessels of Zhongshan".
culture:中山王墓.old: Tomb of the king of Zhongshan

culture:书同文·车同轨.note: Right after unification Qin "made uniform the laws and the standards of weight and length; carts had the same axle width, writing the same characters", with small seal script as the standard, and the currency was unified as the banliang coin.

culture:博浪沙刺秦.note: To avenge Han, Zhang Liang and a strongman ambushed the First Emperor at Bolangsha with an iron mallet weighing a hundred and twenty jin, but struck an attendant carriage by mistake; Zhang Liang fled into hiding at Xiapi.
culture:博浪沙刺秦.old: Attempt on the First Emperor at Bolangsha

culture:吴起变法.note: King Dao of Chu made Wu Qi his chief minister; Wu Qi "made the laws clear and the orders precise, cut unnecessary offices, and stripped distant members of the royal clan of their status". When King Dao died, Wu Qi was shot dead beside the king's body.

culture:商鞅变法.note: Duke Xiao of Qin employed Shang Yang, who carried out two rounds of reform: collective responsibility and denunciation, rewards for farming and fighting, ranks for military merit, abolition of the well-field system and opening of the field boundaries, counties throughout the state, and unified weights and measures. Qin became rich and strong.

culture:孟子故里.note: Mencius was a man of Zou; he counselled King Hui of Liang and King Xuan of Qi, advocating "humane government" and "the people are most important".

culture:屈原投江.note: After the fall of the capital Ying, Qu Yuan drowned himself in the Miluo River. Author of the Li Sao, the Nine Songs, the Heavenly Questions and other works.

culture:庄子故里.note: Zhuang Zhou was a man of Meng in Song, once an official of the lacquer garden, and author of the Zhuangzi.

culture:易水送别.note: Crown Prince Dan and his retainers, dressed in white, saw Jing Ke off on the banks of the Yi River: "The wind sighs, the Yi is cold; the hero, once gone, will not return."

culture:曾侯乙墓.note: Tomb of a ruler of Zeng from the early Warring States; it yielded a 65-piece set of bells spanning five and a half octaves and able to play all twelve pitches of the scale.
culture:曾侯乙墓.old: Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng

culture:李悝变法.note: Marquis Wen of Wei made Li Kui chancellor; Li Kui taught "making full use of the land's strength", introduced the price-stabilising grain purchases and wrote the six-chapter Canon of Laws: the forerunner of the Warring States reforms.

culture:泰山封禅.note: On his eastern tour the First Emperor performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai and the Shan sacrifice at Liangfu, and had stone inscriptions praising the virtue of Qin carved on Mount Tai, the Langya Terrace and elsewhere.
culture:泰山封禅.old: Feng and Shan sacrifices at Mount Tai

culture:灵渠.note: The supervising censor Lu cut a canal linking the Xiang and Li rivers (with the ploughshare divider and the large and small weirs), joining the Yangtze and Pearl river systems, to carry grain for the southern campaign against the Hundred Yue. It is still navigable today.

culture:焚书坑儒.note: Chunyu Yue asked for a return to enfeoffment; Li Si rebutted him and proposed burning the Odes, the Documents and the writings of the Hundred Schools; the next year more than four hundred and sixty scholars were buried alive at Xianyang.
culture:焚书坑儒.old: Burning of books and burying of scholars

culture:申不害相韩.note: Shen Buhai governed Han by "technique": "at home he reformed government and teaching, abroad he dealt with the lords; for fifteen years, until Shenzi's death, the state was well ordered and its army strong".

culture:碣石刻辞.note: On his tour to Jieshi, the First Emperor had an inscription carved saying he had "pulled down city walls, cut through river dykes and levelled strongholds": the walls, forts and dykes between the six states were demolished, and the interior long walls were abandoned after unification as a result.

culture:稷下学宫.note: Qi set up an academy outside the Ji Gate of its capital; Mencius, Xunzi (three times its libationer), Zou Yan, Chunyu Kun, Shen Dao and others gathered there, "not governing but debating": the centre of the contention of the Hundred Schools.

culture:胡服骑射.note: King Wuling of Zhao ordered his people to adopt nomad dress and learn mounted archery, creating a cavalry force that greatly strengthened Zhao's army.

culture:荀子·兰陵.note: In his later years Xunzi was made magistrate of Lanling by Lord Chunshen and spent the rest of his life there writing; Han Fei and Li Si were both his students.

culture:西门豹治邺.note: Ximen Bao ended the custom of "brides for the River Lord" and had the people dig twelve canals to irrigate the land with water from the Zhang River; Ye was well governed.

culture:郑国渠.note: Zheng Guo, a hydraulic engineer from Han, went to Qin to build a canal as a plan to "exhaust Qin"; when the plot came out, Qin still had him finish it. The canal led the Jing River east to the Luo and irrigated more than forty thousand qing of fields: "Guanzhong became fertile land".

culture:郭店楚简.note: Bamboo slips from a Chu tomb, including the earliest known manuscript of the Laozi and several lost Confucian texts.

culture:都江堰.note: Built under Li Bing, Qin governor of Shu: the Fish Mouth divides the river, the Flying Sand Weir sheds floods and the Precious Bottle Neck draws water, making the Chengdu Plain the "Land of Abundance". Still in use today.

culture:阿房宫.note: Since Xianyang was crowded and the palaces of the former kings small, the First Emperor built a court palace in the Shanglin Park south of the Wei River; its front hall was Epang, and it was still unfinished when Qin fell.

culture:骊山陵.note: Mausoleum of the First Emperor of Qin, begun soon after he came to the throne and greatly enlarged after unification by more than seven hundred thousand conscripted convicts; the terracotta army pits lie to its east.

culture:鸿沟.note: King Hui of Wei led water from the He past Xingyang and Daliang and southeast to the Ying, Guo, Sui, Si and other rivers into the Huai: the first large network of artificial canals in the Central Plains.

culture:黄金台.mod: around Yi County – Dingxing, Hebei (location disputed)
culture:黄金台.note: To take revenge on Qi, King Zhao of Yan took Guo Wei as his teacher, "building him a palace and serving him as master"; Yue Yi, Zou Yan and Ju Xin vied to come to Yan.

jun:三川郡.note: Set up after the destruction of East Zhou and the capture of Chenggao and Xingyang; named after the three rivers He, Luo and Yi.

jun:上党郡.note: Set up after Shangdang was retaken in 247 BC.

jun:上郡.note: Wei ceded the fifteen counties of Shang Commandery (328 BC), and Qin kept the commandery.

jun:东海郡.note: Mentioned in the Chen She chapter of the Shiji and elsewhere; generally thought to have been split off after unification (date unknown).

jun:东郡.note: Set up from Suanzao and nineteen other Wei towns, cutting the vertical alliance east of the mountains in two.

jun:临菑郡.note: Set up after the destruction of Qi. Written 临菑 (Linzi) on Qin clay sealings and called Qi Commandery in the Hanshu treatise on geography.

jun:九原郡.mod: Seat: Jiuyuan (W of Baotou, Inner Mongolia)
jun:九原郡.note: Set up after Henandi was taken; the northern end of the Straight Road.

jun:九江郡.note: Set up after the destruction of Chu.

jun:云中郡.mod: Seat: Yunzhong (NE of Togtoh, Inner Mongolia)

jun:代郡.mod: Seat: Dai (NE of Yu County, Hebei)
jun:代郡.note: Set up after the capture of Jia, king of Dai.

jun:会稽郡.note: Set up after the lords of Yue surrendered.

jun:内史.note: The metropolitan region, not organised as a commandery but administered directly by the Neishi.

jun:北地郡.mod: Seat: Yiqu (NW of Ning County, Gansu)
jun:北地郡.note: Set up after the destruction of Yiqu.

jun:南海郡.note: Set up after Lingnan was pacified, with Ren Xiao as commandant and Zhao Tuo as magistrate of Longchuan.

jun:南郡.note: Set up after Bai Qi took Ying.

jun:博阳郡.note: Identified by Hou Xiaorong in Qindai zhengqu dili (one view).

jun:即墨郡.note: A Qin clay sealing reads "governor of Jimo": the Jiaodong region.

jun:右北平郡.note: Taken over from Yan. (One view: its seat was Pinggang, SW of modern Lingyuan, Liaoning.)

jun:四川郡.note: Set up from Chu's lands north of the Huai. Written 四川 (Sichuan) in the Yuelu Academy Qin slips and 泗水 (Sishui) in the Hanshu treatise on geography and the Shuijing zhu. Liu Bang came from Pei County in this commandery.

jun:城阳郡.note: Listed in Wang Guowei's Qin jun kao; a Qin clay sealing reads "Chengyang" (one view).

jun:巨鹿郡.note: Set up from eastern Zhao (date of establishment uncertain).

jun:巴郡.note: Set up after the conquest of Ba.

jun:广阳郡.note: Set up after the Yan capital Ji was taken (one view: Qin had no Guangyang Commandery).

jun:恒山郡.note: Set up from the former Zhongshan lands of Zhao, attested in the Yuelu Academy Qin slips. Renamed Changshan under the Han to avoid the personal name of Emperor Wen.

jun:桂林郡.note: Set up after Lingnan was pacified.

jun:汉中郡.note: Set up from Chu's Hanzhong, taken after the Battle of Danyang.

jun:河东郡.note: Set up after Wei ceded Hedong (c. 290–286 BC).

jun:河内郡.note: Attested in the Yuelu Academy Qin slips; generally thought to have been split off after unification. Its seat, Yewang, was then the residence of Jue, lord of Wey, a Qin dependency.

jun:洞庭郡.mod: Seat: Linyuan (one view); around Changde, Hunan (seat disputed)
jun:洞庭郡.note: A commandery name attested in the Liye and Yuelu Academy Qin slips; Qianling County belonged to Dongting Commandery. Whether the Qianzhong Commandery the Shiji records as set up in 277 BC existed, and how it related to Dongting, is disputed among scholars.

jun:济北郡.note: A Qin clay sealing reads "governor of Jibei"; generally thought to have been split off after unification.

jun:淮阳郡.note: Set up from Chu's Chen region. Called "Chu Commandery" in the Shiji, and sometimes Chen Commandery later.

jun:清河郡.mod: Seat: Qingyang (uncertain); N of Linqing, Shandong (one view)
jun:清河郡.note: The Yuelu Academy Qin slips mention an "acting governor of Qinghe"; its seat was possibly Qingyang, seat of the Han-dynasty Qinghe Commandery.

jun:渔阳郡.note: Taken over from Yan; Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose on their way to garrison duty at Yuyang.

jun:琅邪郡.note: Set up after the destruction of Qi, attested in the Yuelu Academy Qin slips. (It was long thought to have been governed from Langya, modern Huangdao District, Qingdao.)

jun:砀郡.note: Set up from the eastern part of Wei after its destruction.

jun:苍梧郡.mod: Seat: unknown; southern Hunan (seat unknown; placed near Chenzhou for now)
jun:苍梧郡.note: A commandery name attested in the Liye and Yuelu Academy Qin slips, set up from "new lands taken from Jing (Chu)" and covering roughly southern Hunan; its seat is unknown, and both its position and its boundaries on the map are conjectural.

jun:薛郡.note: Set up from the former lands of Lu and Xue.

jun:蜀郡.note: Set up after the conquest of Shu (at first a Marquis of Shu was enfeoffed; from 285 BC a governor was appointed).

jun:衡山郡.note: Attested in the Yuelu Academy Qin slips; generally thought to have been split off after unification.

jun:象郡.note: Set up after Lingnan was pacified. By one view it extended south into north-central Vietnam; by another it lay only in what is now SW Guangxi.

jun:辽东郡.note: Set up after the capture of Xi, king of Yan; written 潦东 in Qin slips.

jun:辽西郡.mod: Seat: Yangle; W of Yi County, Liaoning; one view: W of Jinzhou
jun:辽西郡.note: Taken over from Yan; written 潦西 in Qin slips.

jun:邯郸郡.note: Set up after Zhao was crushed.

jun:长沙郡.note: Set up after Chu's lands south of the Yangtze were pacified.

jun:闽中郡.note: The king of Minyue was reduced to a chieftain and his land made Minzhong Commandery, in practice a loose-rein arrangement.

jun:颍川郡.note: Set up after the destruction of Han.

pass:井陉.note: The fifth of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, linking the Zhao capital with the Taiyuan basin. Wang Jian's army came out this way when Qin destroyed Zhao.

pass:伊阙.note: Two hills facing each other like gate towers with the Yi River flowing between: Luoyang's southern gate.

pass:冥阸.mod: S of Xinyang, Henan (around Pingjing Pass)
pass:冥阸.note: Also written Mengsai, or Ming'e with different characters; a fortress on Chu's northern frontier, one of the "Three Passes of Yiyang".

pass:函谷关.note: Qin's eastern gate, the "stronghold of Xiao and Hangu". The allied armies that attacked Qin in 318 and 241 BC were both stopped here; in 298 BC Qi, Han and Wei did break through Hangu.

pass:句注塞.note: Around the later Yanmen Pass; a fortress on Zhao's northern frontier.

pass:太行陉.mod: Tianjing Pass, S of Jincheng, Shanxi
pass:太行陉.note: The second of the Eight Passes of the Taihang (the Yangchang slope road), the main route north from Yewang to Shangdang. In 262 BC Qin took Yewang and cut Shangdang's southern road.

pass:孟津.mod: NE of Mengjin District, Luoyang, Henan
pass:孟津.note: Yellow River ford north of Luoyang; by tradition King Wu of Zhou gathered the lords here in his campaign against King Zhou of Shang.

pass:居庸塞.note: The eighth of the Eight Passes of the Taihang (Jundu Pass), Yan's northern gateway.

pass:峣关.note: Also called the Lantian Pass, the last pass on the Wu Pass road before Guanzhong.

pass:成皋.note: The later Hulao Pass, the gateway east from Luoyang; a Han stronghold.

pass:扞关.mod: E of Fengjie, Chongqing (one view: Changyang, Hubei)
pass:扞关.note: Chu's pass against Ba and Shu in the west.

pass:散关.note: The Great San Pass, at the northern end of the Chencang Road through the Qinling, one of the routes into Hanzhong and Ba–Shu.

pass:武关.note: Qin's southern gate, leading to Nanyang and the Yangtze–Han region. In 299 BC King Huai of Chu went through the Wu Pass to meet King Zhao of Qin, was detained, and died while detained in Qin.

pass:滏口陉.note: The fourth of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, the route west from Handan to Shangdang.

pass:白马津.note: Important ford on the ancient Yellow River SW of Puyang.

pass:萧关.note: The northwestern gateway to Guanzhong, commanding the route along the upper Jing River; a defence against Yiqu and the northern nomads.

pass:蒲阪津.note: Yellow River ford between Hedong and Guanzhong (Pujin).

pass:轵关陉.note: The first of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, leading west from Henei to Hedong.

pass:飞狐陉.mod: between Laiyuan and Yu County, Hebei
pass:飞狐陉.note: The seventh of the Eight Passes of the Taihang, linking Dai with the heartlands of Yan and Zhao.

pass:高阙.mod: SE of Urad Rear Banner, Inner Mongolia
pass:高阙.note: A gap in the Yin Mountains, the fortress at the western end of the Zhao Northern Long Wall.

people:东瓯.note: A branch of the Yue, living in the Ou River valley of southern Zhejiang.

people:东胡.note: A nomadic people of the northeast, crushed by the Yan general Qin Kai and driven back more than a thousand li.

people:东胡#2.note: A nomadic people of the northeast.

people:匈奴.note: Nomadic people who rose north and south of the Yin Mountains in the late Warring States; Zhao, Yan and Qin all built long walls against them.

people:夜郎.note: The largest tribal state among the Southwestern Yi.

people:朝鲜.note: Gija Joseon, bordering Yan at Manbanhan (around the modern Cheongcheon River).

people:林胡.note: A northern nomadic people, crushed by King Wuling of Zhao; its land passed to Zhao.

people:楼烦.note: A northern people skilled in mounted archery, crushed by King Wuling of Zhao; they moved north to the Hetao.

people:楼烦#2.note: After moving north the Loufan lived south of the Hetao; after the Qin unification Meng Tian drove them out.

people:氐.note: Lived in the mountains of southern Gansu and northern Sichuan.

people:滇.note: Around 279 BC the Chu general Zhuang Qiao led an army to Dian; when Qin cut off his way home he "changed his dress, followed their customs and ruled over them".

people:羌.note: The Western Qiang tribes, living in the He–Huang region and west of Longxi.

people:西瓯.note: The Yue of Lingnan. During the Qin southern campaign Yixusong, lord of the Xi'ou, was killed; the Yue fled into the mountains and forests, raided the Qin army at night and killed its commander Tu Sui; the region was pacified only in 214 BC.

people:越人诸君长.note: After Chu destroyed Yue around 306 BC, the princes of the Yue royal house scattered along the coast south of the Zhe River, "some as kings, some as lords", each ruling on his own while paying court to Chu; Yue was no longer a state. In 222 BC Wang Jian "received the surrender of the lords of Yue" and made their land Kuaiji Commandery.

people:闽越.note: A branch of the Yue, living in modern Fujian.

range:中条山.note: The southern screen of the Hedong basin; Lake Xie (the salt lake) at its northern foot was a source of Wei's wealth.

range:五岭.note: Chu's southern frontier stopped roughly at the northern foot of the Five Ridges; south of the ridges was the land of the Hundred Yue, and only after the Qin unification (214 BC) were the three Lingnan commanderies opened.

range:伏牛山.note: Northern screen of the Nanyang basin; the Chu Fangcheng was built along its spurs.

range:会稽山.note: Birthplace of the state of Yue; by tradition Yu the Great was buried at Kuaiji.

range:医巫闾山.note: The guardian mountain of ancient Youzhou, within Yan's Liaoxi Commandery.

range:华山.note: Anciently called Taihua, the Western Peak. The southern end of the Qin–Wei struggle for Hexi.

range:南山.note: Anciently called the Nan Mountains or the Zhongnan Mountains, the southern screen of Guanzhong. Between Guanzhong and Hanzhong it could only be crossed by the Chencang, Baoxie, Tangluo, Ziwu and other valley roads.

range:吕梁山.note: The western barrier of Shanxi and Zhao's western border.

range:大别山.note: The barrier between the Yangtze and the Huai; Ming'e and the other "Three Passes of Yiyang" lie at its western end.

range:大巴山.note: The barrier between Hanzhong and Ba–Shu; Qin's attack on Shu went by the Jinniu (Shiniu) Road.

range:太行山.note: The range between Shanxi and Hebei, stretching eight hundred li from north to south. Its "Eight Passes of the Taihang" were the east–west routes, and much of the fighting between Qin and Zhao, and Qin and Wei, followed them.

range:岷山.note: The ancients took the Min Mountains as the source of the Jiang; Yu Gong: "from the Min Mountains he led the Jiang".

range:崤山.note: With the Hangu Pass, the "stronghold of Xiao and Hangu", the throat of Qin's route east.

range:嵩山.note: Anciently called Taishi or Waifang, the Central Peak; the heartland of Han.

range:巫山.note: Site of the Three Gorges of the Yangtze; Chu set up Wu Commandery to block the way east out of Ba–Shu.

range:恒山.note: The ancient Northern Peak (before the Han the Northern Peak was around Mount Damao in modern Quyang, Hebei). Mount Gouzhu to its west was Yanmen, Zhao's northern gate.

range:桐柏山.note: Source of the Huai River, on Chu's northern frontier.

range:武夷山.note: The barrier between Minyue and the interior.

range:武陵山.note: The uplands where Chu's Qianzhong Commandery lay.

range:泰山·沂山.note: Mount Tai, anciently called Daizong, is the Eastern Peak; the Qi Long Wall was built along its northern foot, marking the border of Qi with Lu and Chu.

range:燕山.note: Yan's northern screen. After King Zhao of Yan, Yan's territory crossed the Yan Mountains and reached Liaodong.

range:贺兰山.note: Where the northern nomadic peoples roamed.

range:阴山.note: King Wuling of Zhao built the Zhao Northern Long Wall along the Yin Mountains west to Gaoque; north of the mountains lay the Xiongnu pastures.

range:陇山.note: The divide between Guanzhong and Longxi, where "the Long slope winds nine times"; the Xiao Pass is at its northern mouth.

river:丹水.note: The Battle of Danyang was fought here (312 BC).

river:云梦泽.mod: Jianghan Plain (Honghu and nearby lakes are its remnants)
river:云梦泽.note: Hunting ground of the kings of Chu: "the marsh of Yunmeng, nine hundred li square" (accounts of its extent vary).

river:伊水.note: Flows north through Yique into the Luo.

river:圃田泽.note: A great marsh of Wei, the regulating lake for the Honggou's water supply.

river:大野泽.note: Also called the Juye Marsh, on the course of the Ji; modern Dongping Lake is its remnant.

river:大陆泽.mod: between Longyao and Julu, Hebei (silted up)
river:大陆泽.note: The ancient Julu Marsh, a great marsh in Zhao.

river:巢湖.note: A large lake in Chu between the Yangtze and the Huai.

river:延江.note: Also called the Fuling River; Zhi (Fuling) was on the border of Ba and Chu.

river:彭蠡泽.note: Forerunner of modern Poyang Lake (the ancient Pengli Marsh did not cover quite the same area as the modern lake).

river:易水.note: Yan's southern border, along which the Yan Southern Long Wall was built; Jing Ke took leave of Yan on the Yi.

river:汉水.note: Its upper course is called the Mian. Hanzhong and Shangyong lie in its basin; Chu "has the Han River for its moat".

river:江.note: In the Warring States "Jiang" meant the Yangtze alone. Its mouth was then around modern Yangzhou and Zhenjiang, with a wide estuary below.

river:江（岷江）.note: The ancients regarded the Min River as the true source of the Yangtze; Dujiangyan was built where it leaves the mountains.

river:汶水.note: One of the border rivers between Qi and Lu.

river:汾水.note: The axis of central Shanxi and Hedong; both Jinyang and Pingyang lie on the Fen.

river:沁水.note: Rises in the Taiyue Mountains and cuts south through the Taihang to the He.

river:沅水.note: The main valley of Chu's Qianzhong Commandery.

river:河.mod: Yellow River (lower course: Warring States channel)
river:河.note: First of the Four Waterways, called simply "He" in the Warring States. Its lower course was very different from today's: roughly from Suxukou in modern Xun County it flowed north past Neihuang, Guantao, Linqing, Dezhou and Cangzhou into the Bohai around modern Huanghua (following Tan Qixiang's reconstruction; schematic), and was the border river between Qi, Zhao and Yan. The modern course (dashed) is the result of many later shifts.

river:治水.note: Also called the Lei River; it flowed through Dai and south of Ji, the Yan capital.

river:泗水.note: Flows south past Qufu and Pengcheng into the Huai; the "twelve lords on the Si" lay in its basin.

river:泾水.note: "The Jing and the Wei are clearly distinct"; the Zhengguo Canal led water from the Jing east to the Luo.

river:洛水.note: The border river in the Qin–Wei struggle for Hexi; Wei built the Wei Hexi Long Wall along the Luo, and Duke Jian of Qin "dug a moat along the Luo".

river:洞庭.note: Zhanguo ce: "south of Chu are Dongting and Cangwu"; in the Warring States the lake was far smaller than in later times.

river:济水.note: One of the Four Waterways; it left the He at Xingyang and flowed east, passing north of Dingtao and through the Juye Marsh, then northeast past the north of modern Jinan to the sea. The place names Jinan, Jiyang and Jining all come from it; it disappeared after the Yellow River captured its course.

river:浙江.note: The name Zhejiang originally referred to this river; after destroying Yue, Chu "took all the old lands of Wu up to the Zhe River".

river:淇水.note: A famous river of Wey; Odes, "Airs of Wey": "Look at that bend of the Qi".

river:淮水.note: One of the Four Waterways, "Jiang, Huai, He and Ji". In the Warring States the lower Huai flowed on its own past Huaiyin to the sea, and there was no Hongze Lake yet; it was the main axis of Chu's eastward expansion.

river:淯水.note: The main river of the Nanyang basin, flowing south past Wan into the Han.

river:渭水.note: The lifeline of Guanzhong; the Qin capital Xianyang stood on the Wei.

river:湘水.note: The main axis of Chu's development of its southern frontier.

river:滹沱.note: The main river of Zhongshan, flowing east into the He.

river:漳水.note: The border river between Zhao and Wei; Ximen Bao irrigated Ye from the Zhang; the Zhao Southern Long Wall was built along the Zhang and the Fu.

river:澧水.note: "On the Yuan there is angelica, on the Li there are orchids."

river:灵渠.note: Cut by the supervising censor Lu, leading water from the Xiang River into the Li River and joining the Yangtze and Pearl river systems; the Qin army relied on it to bring up grain and pacify Lingnan.

river:西汉水.note: Called the Xihan River in its upper course and the Yu River in its lower course; the heartland of Ba.

river:西海.note: Ancient name of Qinghai Lake, pastureland of the Qiang.

river:资水.note: A river on Chu's southern frontier.

river:辽水.note: Western boundary of Yan's Liaodong Commandery.

river:邗沟.note: Dug by Fuchai, king of Wu, in 486 BC, running north from Guangling (Yangzhou) to the Huai; one of the earliest canals with a firm date.

river:郑国渠.note: Begun in 246 BC, leading water from the Jing at Jingyang east into the Luo, more than three hundred li long.

river:雒水.note: The Yi–Luo valley was the seat of the Zhou royal domain; Yiyang and Luoyang both lie on this river.

river:雷夏泽.note: An ancient marsh; by tradition Shun fished in the Lei Marsh.

river:震泽.note: Modern Lake Tai, also called Juqu, between Wu and Yue.

river:颍水.note: Rises on Mount Song and flows past Yangzhai and south of Chen into the Huai; the southern section of the Honggou joined the Ying.

river:鸿沟.note: Dug from 360 BC under King Hui of Wei, leading water from the He at Xingyang east past Daliang, then south to Chen and into the Ying, linking the He and the Huai. In the Chu–Han contention the Honggou served as the boundary.

road:五尺道.note: Cut by Chang E, running south from Bodao (modern Yibin) to Yelang and Lake Dian; because the mountain road was steep and narrow it was only five feet wide.

road:直道.note: Built under Meng Tian, running north from Yunyang (the Ganquan Palace) along the Ziwu Ridge straight to Jiuyuan, "cutting through hills and filling valleys for eighteen hundred li"; cavalry could ride from Xianyang to the Yin Mountains within three days.

road:驰道.note: The trunk roads of the realm, built with Xianyang at their centre, "reaching Yan and Qi in the east and Wu and Chu in the south", fifty paces wide and planted with a tree every three zhang (Hanshu, biography of Jia Shan). The routes are schematic.

state:中山.mod: Ji surname (Xianyu of the White Di)
state:中山.note:
Capitals: Gu → Lingshou. A "state of a thousand chariots", wedged between Yan and Zhao.
In 406 BC the Wei general Yue Yang destroyed Zhongshan, which was restored around 380 BC; in 323 BC it joined Wei, Han, Zhao and Yan in "five states hailing one another as kings".
The tomb of King Cuo of Zhongshan yielded bronzes inlaid with gold and silver, the "Three Vessels of Zhongshan" and more, unsurpassed in craftsmanship in their day.
King Wuling of Zhao destroyed Zhongshan in 296 BC.

state:义渠.note:
One of the Western Rong, who lived in walled towns in what is now Qingyang in Gansu and southern Ningxia, and fought Qin for a long time.
In 272 BC Queen Dowager Xuan of Qin lured the king of Yiqu to the Ganquan Palace and killed him; Qin sent troops to destroy Yiqu, set up the Longxi, Beidi and Shang commanderies, and built a long wall against the Hu.

state:卫.note:
Capital: Diqiu (Puyang). Reduced to a small state in the Warring States, a dependent first of Wei, then of Qin.
Shang Yang, Wu Qi, Lü Buwei and Jing Ke all came from Wey.
In 241 BC Qin took Puyang and set up Dong Commandery, moving Jue, lord of Wey, to Yewang; Wey survived as a Qin dependency until 209 BC, when the Second Emperor of Qin reduced its lord to a commoner: the last of the Zhou fiefs to fall.

state:周（王畿）.note:
Common sovereign of all under Heaven, but in the Warring States left with only a corner of land around Luoyang.
In 367 BC Zhou split into two small states, West Zhou (capital Wangcheng at Henan) and East Zhou (capital Gong).
In 256 BC Qin destroyed West Zhou, King Nan of Zhou died, and the Nine Tripods went to Qin; in 249 BC the Qin chancellor Lü Buwei destroyed East Zhou. The Zhou dynasty, which had lasted some eight hundred years, came to an end.

state:宋.mod: Zi surname (descendants of the Shang kings)
state:宋.note:
Capital: Shangqiu (Suiyang). In the east of the Central Plains, rich but surrounded by enemies.
Yan, ruler of Song (King Kang), took the title of king; he "shot at Heaven and flogged the Earth", and the lords called him "the Jie of Song".
In 286 BC King Min of Qi destroyed Song, whose lands were later divided between Wei and Chu; the destruction of Song directly provoked the five-state attack on Qi.
Zhuangzi was a man of Meng in Song; according to one view, Mozi was also from Song.

state:巴.mod: Ji surname (one view: descendants of Lord Lin)
state:巴.note:
Capital: Jiangzhou (modern Chongqing), later also Langzhong. The Ba were brave and fierce warriors, famous for the Ba–Yu dance.
Hereditary enemies of Shu. In 316 BC Sima Cuo and Zhang Yi of Qin took advantage of the war between Ba and Shu, destroyed Shu and then Ba, and set up Ba Commandery.

state:楚.note:
Capitals: Ying (Jinancheng) → Chen (278 BC) → Juyang (253 BC) → Shouchun (241 BC).
The largest state of the Warring States: it held the Yangtze–Han and Yangtze–Huai regions, reached the Five Ridges in the south, and after destroying Yue held all the old lands of Wu and Yue in the east.
Reforms: King Dao of Chu had Wu Qi carry out reforms (c. 386–381 BC); after Dao's death Wu Qi was shot dead by the old nobility and the reforms were abandoned.
Notable rulers: King Dao; King Wei (defeated Yue in 333 BC and crushed Qi at Xuzhou in the north); King Huai (destroyed Yue and set up Jiangdong Commandery c. 306 BC; later deceived by Zhang Yi, he died while detained in Qin); King Qingxiang; King Kaolie.
People: Wu Qi, Qu Yuan, Shao Hua (who went to Yue to sow discord), Lord Chunshen Huang Xie, Zhuang Qiao (who entered Dian), Xiang Yan.
In 223 BC Wang Jian and Meng Wu crushed Chu at Qinan and captured Fuchu, king of Chu; in 222 BC Qin pacified Chu's lands south of the Yangtze.

state:燕.note:
Capitals: Ji (Upper Capital); Wuyang (Lower Capital, modern Yi County).
In 314 BC King Kuai of Yan ceded the throne to Zizhi, throwing the state into chaos, and King Xuan of Qi seized the chance to crush Yan. King Zhao of Yan built the Golden Terrace to attract talent, and Yue Yi, Guo Wei, Zou Yan and Ju Xin all came.
Around 300 BC the Yan general Qin Kai made a surprise attack on the Donghu and routed them, who fell back more than a thousand li; Yan set up the five commanderies of Shanggu, Yuyang, Youbeiping, Liaoxi and Liaodong and built a long wall from Zaoyang to Xiangping.
In 284 BC Yue Yi crushed Qi and almost destroyed it. In 227 BC Crown Prince Dan sent Jing Ke to assassinate the king of Qin.
In 226 BC Qin took Ji, and Xi, king of Yan, fled to Liaodong; in 222 BC Wang Ben attacked Liaodong and captured him.

state:秦.note:
Capitals: Yong → Yueyang (383 BC) → Xianyang (350 BC).
Reforms: Duke Xiao of Qin had Shang Yang carry out two rounds of reform (356 and 350 BC): the well-field system was abolished and the field boundaries opened, counties were instituted, farming and fighting were rewarded, and a twenty-rank scale of military merit was created.
Notable rulers: Duke Xiao, King Huiwen (took the title of king in 324 BC), King Wu, King Zhaoxiang, King Zheng of Qin.
Generals and ministers: Shang Yang, Zhang Yi, Sima Cuo, Wei Ran, Fan Ju ("ally with the distant, attack the near"), Bai Qi, Lü Buwei, Wang Jian, Wang Ben, Li Si.
Expansion: 330–328 BC gained Wei's Hexi and Shang Commandery; 316 BC conquered Ba and Shu; 312 BC took Hanzhong; 278 BC took Ying and set up Nan Commandery; 272 BC destroyed Yiqu; 260 BC Battle of Changping; 256 and 249 BC destroyed the two Zhou; 230–221 BC destroyed all six states within ten years.
In 221 BC Qin unified the realm; King Zheng took the title First Emperor and divided the realm into thirty-six commanderies.
Expansion continued after unification: in 215 BC Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu north and took Henandi; in 214 BC Jiuyuan Commandery was set up and the old long walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan were joined into the "Great Wall"; the same year Lingnan was pacified and the Nanhai, Guilin and Xiang commanderies were set up. The imperial highways and the Straight Road were built and the Lingqu Canal cut. The First Emperor died at Shaqiu in 210 BC; Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose in 209 BC; Qin fell in 207 BC.

state:苴.mod: Kaiming lineage (brother of the king of Shu)
state:苴.note:
Capital: Jiameng (modern Zhaohua, Guangyuan, Sichuan). According to the Shu treatise of the Huayang guozhi, the king of Shu "enfeoffed his younger brother Jiameng separately in Hanzhong, with the title Marquis of Ju, and named his town Jiameng"; it guarded the northern gateway of Shu at a key point on the Jinniu (Shiniu) Road.
The Marquis of Ju was on good terms with the king of Ba, while Ba and Shu were hereditary enemies. The king of Shu attacked Ju in anger, the Marquis of Ju fled to Ba, and Ba and Ju appealed to Qin for help.
In 316 BC King Huiwen of Qin sent Sima Cuo and Zhang Yi down the Stone Ox Road against Shu; after destroying Shu they "went on to take Ju and Ba". Ju was the direct trigger of the Qin conquest of Ba and Shu, and lasted no more than a few decades.
The "Hanzhong" of "enfeoffed in Hanzhong" is Chang Qu's broad usage: he also placed Jiameng in his Hanzhong treatise. Ju's territory lay around Jiameng on the upper Jialing River, while Nanzheng in the Hanzhong basin remained under the direct rule of the king of Shu, so that Ju split Shu into northern and southern parts. Whether the area around Ningqiang and Lüeyang belonged to Ju or to Shu is not recorded; the map shows it only schematically.

state:蜀.note:
Capital: Chengdu. A thousand li of fertile land, which after the Qin conquest became the granary of the wars of unification.
To the north lay the Hanzhong basin: the Huayang guozhi says that in the time of King Xian of Zhou "the king of Shu held the lands of Bao and Han", and that after conquering Shu, Qin "divided off parts of Ba and Shu to set up Hanzhong Commandery".
In 316 BC King Huiwen of Qin followed Sima Cuo's advice, attacked Shu by the Jinniu (Shiniu) Road, destroyed it and set up Shu Commandery.
Around 256–251 BC Li Bing, the Qin governor of Shu, built Dujiangyan, so that on the Chengdu Plain "flood and drought obey man, and famine is unknown".

state:赵.note:
Capitals: Jinyang → Zhongmou (425 BC) → Handan (386 BC). In 403 BC recognised as a feudal lord together with Han and Wei (the partition of Jin).
King Wuling of Zhao adopted nomad dress and mounted archery (307 BC), destroyed Zhongshan (296 BC), crushed the Linhu and Loufan in the north, set up the Yunzhong, Yanmen and Dai commanderies, and built a long wall reaching Gaoque.
Lin Xiangru returned the jade disc intact to Zhao, and the general and the minister were reconciled; Zhao She won at Yuyu; the crushing defeat at Changping in 260 BC left Zhao badly weakened.
Li Mu crushed the Xiongnu in the north and repelled mighty Qin in the south (at Fei and Powu); in 229 BC Qin sowed discord, and Qian, king of Zhao, had Li Mu killed.
In 228 BC Qin took Handan and captured King Qian; Prince Jia fled to Dai and styled himself king of Dai; Dai fell in 222 BC.

state:越.note:
Capitals: Kuaiji → Langya (468 BC) → Wu (379 BC; Bamboo Annals: "in the 33rd year of Yi, viscount of Yue, he moved to Wu"). After Goujian destroyed Wu (473 BC), Yue was hegemon of the southeast.
In the Warring States it was riven by repeated internal strife; the Zhuangzi says "the people of Yue killed their rulers three generations running": in 375 BC Crown Prince Zhujiu killed Yi, king of Yue, and around 365 BC Si, younger brother of Si'ou, killed Mang'an, king of Yue.
In 312 BC the king of Yue still sent envoys to Wei with a state barge, three hundred boats, five million arrows, rhinoceros horn and ivory (Bamboo Annals), showing that Yue was then still a kingdom of substance.
There are two views of when it fell: (1) the traditional view, based on the Yue chapter of the Shiji and the Zizhi Tongjian, that in 334/333 BC King Wei of Chu routed Yue and killed Wujiang, king of Yue; (2) Yang Kuan and others, from the biography of Gan Mao in the Shiji, Fan Huan's words in the Chu section of the Zhanguo ce, Zhao Ju's words in the Chu chapter of the Shiji, and the Hanfeizi's "Zhao Hua … within five years was able to destroy Yue", conclude that King Huai of Chu sent Shao Hua into Yue to stir up internal strife, destroyed Yue in the turmoil around 306 BC, killed Wujiang, took all the old lands of Wu up to the Zhe River, and set up Jiangdong Commandery. This map follows the 306 BC view and treats the battle of 333 BC as an earlier stage of the Chu–Yue wars.
Afterwards the Yue people scattered along the coast south of the Zhe River, "some as kings, some as lords, on the coast south of the Yangtze, paying court to Chu"; in 222 BC Wang Jian "received the surrender of the lords of Yue and set up Kuaiji Commandery". The Dong'ou and Minyue were their descendants.

state:韩.note:
Capitals: Pingyang → Yiyang → Yangzhai → Xinzheng (moved there after destroying Zheng in 375 BC).
The weakest of the seven powers, a "land open to war on all four sides": mighty Qin to the west, and Wei, Zhao and Chu surrounding it to the east, north and south.
Marquis Zhao of Han made Shen Buhai chancellor (355–337 BC), governing by "technique"; "the state was well ordered and its army strong, and no one invaded Han".
In 262 BC Qin cut Shangdang off from the Han heartland, and Feng Ting, governor of Shangdang, surrendered the territory to Zhao, setting off the Battle of Changping. Han sent the hydraulic engineer Zheng Guo to build a canal in Qin to "exhaust Qin", but it only made Qin richer and stronger.
Han Fei was a prince of Han. In 230 BC Teng, the Neishi, attacked Han, captured An, king of Han, and set up Yingchuan Commandery: the first of the six states to fall.

state:魏.note:
Capitals: Anyi → Daliang (361 BC, or 364 BC), hence Wei was also called "Liang".
Marquis Wen of Wei employed Li Kui to carry out reforms, Wu Qi to take Hexi, Ximen Bao to govern Ye and Yue Yang to destroy Zhongshan, making Wei the strongest state of the early Warring States.
King Hui of Wei (King Hui of Liang) dominated the Central Plains, but after two defeats by Qi at Guiling and Maling and the loss of Hexi and Shang Commandery to Qin, Wei went into decline.
Wei cut the Honggou Canal, linking the He and the Huai. In the late Warring States Lord Xinling stole the tally to rescue Zhao and led a vertical alliance that defeated Qin at Hewai.
In 225 BC Wang Ben flooded Daliang with water from the He and the Honggou, and Jia, king of Wei, surrendered.

state:鲁.note:
Capital: Qufu. Ruled by the descendants of the Duke of Zhou; a land of ritual and music, Confucius's home state and the centre of Confucian learning. Weak in the Warring States.
In 256 BC King Kaolie of Chu destroyed Lu (one view: in 249 BC, moving Duke Qing of Lu to Ju / Xiayi).

state:齐.note:
Capital: Linzi. In 386 BC Tian He was recognised as a feudal lord, and the Tian lineage replaced the Jiang house of Qi.
King Wei of Qi had Zou Ji carry out reforms and founded the Jixia Academy, where the Hundred Schools gathered.
Defeated Wei twice, at Guiling (353 BC) and Maling (341 BC), and stood as Qin's equal in the east; in 288 BC King Min of Qi and King Zhao of Qin styled themselves Emperor of the East and Emperor of the West.
Destroyed Song in 286 BC; in 284 BC overrun by the five-state coalition led by the Yan general Yue Yi, keeping only Ju and Jimo; in 279 BC Tian Dan restored the state with his fire-ox formation, but Qi was greatly weakened.
People: Zou Ji, Tian Ji, Sun Bin, Lord Mengchang Tian Wen, Tian Dan, Lu Zhonglian.
In 221 BC Wang Ben attacked Qi southward from Yan; Jian, king of Qi, surrendered without a fight, and the last of the six states was gone.

town:下邳.note: Where Zhang Liang later went into hiding and met the Old Man of the Yellow Stone.

town:东武城.note: Fief of Lord Pingyuan, Zhao Sheng of Zhao.

town:临晋.note: Key place in Hexi between Qin and Wei, at a Yellow River ford.

town:临邛.note: Walled by Zhang Ruo after the Qin conquest of Shu; later the Zhuo family grew rich here smelting iron.

town:云阳.note: Site of the Qin Ganquan Palace; Han Fei died in prison at Yunyang (233 BC).

town:令支.note: Originally Lingzhi, a state of the Shan Rong.

town:共.note: After surrendering to Qin, Jian, king of Qi, was moved to Gong and starved to death among the pines and cypresses.

town:冀.note: With Gui, one of the earliest counties (688 BC).

town:历下.note: Key place in western Qi; both Yue Yi's invasion of Qi and Han Xin's surprise attack on Qi passed this way.

town:召陵.mod: E of Yancheng District, Luohe, Henan
town:召陵.note: Where Duke Huan of Qi made a covenant with Chu (656 BC).

town:叶.note: Fief of Shen Zhuliang, the Lord of She in the fable "The Lord of She Loves Dragons".

town:夷陵.note: Site of the tombs of the Chu kings, burned by Bai Qi in 278 BC.

town:孤竹.note: The state of Boyi and Shuqi.

town:宁新中.note: Taken by Qin (257 BC) and renamed Anyang.

town:安陆.note: Where the Shuihudi Qin slips were found.

town:少梁.note: Fought over repeatedly by Qin and Wei in Hexi; Qin renamed it Xiayang.

town:屯留.mod: S of Tunliu District, Changzhi, Shanxi
town:屯留.note: Chengjiao, Lord Chang'an, rebelled against Qin at Tunliu (239 BC).

town:巫.note: Seat of Chu's Wu Commandery; passed to Qin in 277 BC.

town:平刚.note: Seat of Yan's Youbeiping Commandery (one view).

town:平城.note: Key place between Zhao's Yanmen and Dai commanderies.

town:平舆.note: The Qin general Wang Jian took the land from Chen south to Pingyu (224 BC).

town:延陵.note: Fief of Ji Zha of Wu.

town:怀.note: Taken by Qin (266 BC): the start of "ally with the distant, attack the near".

town:息.note: The ancient state of Xi, destroyed by King Wen of Chu.

town:房陵.note: Qin moved Lao Ai's retainers and Qian, king of Zhao, to Fangling.

town:新蔡.note: One of the later capitals of Cai.

town:方城.note: Fangcheng of Yan, not the Chu Fangcheng.

town:无终.note: Originally Wuzhong, a state of the Shan Rong; later part of Yan.

town:曲沃.note: Ancestral town of the house of Jin.

town:朝歌.note: Old capital of King Zhou of Shang, later an early capital of Wey.

town:杜.note: One of the earlier counties set up by Qin (687 BC).

town:枳.note: Site of the tombs of the Ba kings.

town:武安.note: Fought over by Qin and Zhao.

town:汧.note: One of the early capitals of the Qin people.

town:汲.note: Under the Western Jin the Bamboo Annals were found in the Ji tomb, a Wei tomb at this place.

town:汾阴.note: Where the Fen River meets the Yellow River.

town:沅陵.note: In the heart of Chu's Qianzhong Commandery; Qianling, where the Liye Qin slips were found, lies to its west.

town:河间.note: Lü Buwei received ten towns of Zhao's Hejian as his fief.

town:渑池.note: Site of the meeting of Qin and Zhao at Mianchi (279 BC), where Lin Xiangru forced the king of Qin to strike an earthenware fou.

town:温.note: The ancient state of Wen, a key town in Henei.

town:滕.note: The state of Teng, whose Duke Wen asked Mencius about government.

town:番.note: Southeastern frontier of Chu (Lord of Po).

town:皖.note: Origin of "Wan", the short name for Anhui.

town:相.note: One of the old capitals of Song.

town:碣石.note: A famous coastal mountain on Yan's eastern frontier, later climbed by both the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of Han.

town:离石.note: Fought over repeatedly by Qin and Zhao.

town:穰.note: Fief of the Qin chancellor Wei Ran, styled Marquis of Rang.

town:端氏.note: After the partition of Jin, the ruler of Jin was moved to Duanshi.

town:绛.note: Xintian, the old capital of Jin and the last residence of the Jin ducal house.

town:罗.note: Chu moved the remnant people of the state of Luo here; the Miluo River, where Qu Yuan drowned himself, flows through it.

town:聊城.note: A Yan general held Liaocheng; Lu Zhonglian shot a letter into the city, and the Yan general killed himself.

town:西垂.note: Early homeland of the Qin people, with the great tombs of the Qin dukes.

town:解.note: On Lake Xie (the salt lake); home town of Guan Yu.

town:豳.note: Where Gong Liu, ancestor of the Zhou, lived.

town:造阳.mod: N of Huailai, Hebei (one view: Dushikou)
town:造阳.note: Western starting point of the Yan Northern Long Wall.

town:邹.note: Capital of Zhu and home town of Mencius.

town:邽.note: In 688 BC Duke Wu of Qin attacked the Gui Rong and Ji Rong and first made their lands counties, among the earliest counties on record in China.

town:郫.note: Duyu (Emperor Wang) of ancient Shu had his capital at Pi.

town:郯.note: The ancient state of Tan, destroyed by Yue (c. 414 BC).

town:郴.note: Southern frontier of Chu; Qin set up Chen County.

town:鄄.note: "Between E and Juan", the birthplace of Sun Bin.

town:鄚.note: Home town of the famous physician Bian Que (one view).

town:鄢陵.note: Site of the Spring and Autumn Battle of Yanling between Jin and Chu.

town:酸枣.note: Qin took Suanzao and nineteen other Wei towns and set up Dong Commandery (242 BC).

town:钱唐.note: Qin set up Qiantang County, which gave the Qiantang River its name.

town:阳城.note: Home town of Chen Sheng (one view). Taken by Qin (256 BC).

town:陕.note: Taken by Qin (324 BC), commanding the eastern mouth of the Xiao–Hangu route.

town:项.note: Where the family of Xiang Yan and Xiang Yu came from.

town:高奴.note: Key town of Shang Commandery, where the "Gaonu bronze one-shi weight for grain" was found.

town:黄.note: The ancient state of Huang (of the Lai Yi).

wall:楚方城.note: The defences of Chu's northern frontier: "Chu has Fangcheng for its wall and the Han River for its moat". Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").
wall:楚方城.yt: built in the Spring and Autumn period, still in use in the Warring States

wall:燕北长城.mod: Zhangjiakou, Hebei – Chifeng, Inner Mongolia – Liaoyang, Liaoning
wall:燕北长城.note: After Qin Kai drove back the Donghu, Yan "built a long wall from Zaoyang to Xiangping" and set up five commanderies against the Hu. After the Qin unification it became the eastern section of the Great Wall.

wall:燕南长城.mod: Yi County – Wen'an, Hebei (Yi River Long Wall)
wall:燕南长城.note: Built along the Yi River against Qi, Zhao and Zhongshan. Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").

wall:秦始皇长城（新筑段）.mod: Lanzhou, Gansu – Ningxia – Hetao and Yin Mountains, Inner Mongolia
wall:秦始皇长城（新筑段）.note: After taking Henandi, Meng Tian "used the river as a barrier", setting up watchtowers and stockades along the Yellow River; he also crossed the river and built walls and forts around the Yin Mountains and Gaoque, joining them with the old long walls of King Zhao of Qin, Zhao and Yan into the "Great Wall", from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east.

wall:秦昭王长城.mod: Lintao, Gansu – Guyuan, Ningxia – Yulin, Shaanxi
wall:秦昭王长城.note: Built after the destruction of Yiqu, from Lintao in the west through Guyuan, Huan County, Wuqi and Jingbian to Yulin and Shenmu, against the northern Hu. After the Qin unification it became the western section of the Great Wall.
wall:秦昭王长城.old: Long Wall of King Zhao of Qin

wall:赵北长城.mod: Zhangjiakou, Hebei – Yin Mountains, Inner Mongolia – Gaoque
wall:赵北长城.note: After crushing the Linhu and Loufan, King Wuling of Zhao "built a long wall from Dai along the foot of the Yin Mountains to Gaoque as a barrier". After the Qin unification it was taken into the Great Wall.

wall:赵南长城.mod: Handan – Ci County, Hebei, between the Zhang and Fu rivers
wall:赵南长城.note: Built by Marquis Su of Zhao between the Zhang and Fu rivers against Wei and Qi. Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").

wall:魏河南长城.note: Built by Wei west of Daliang against Han and Qin. Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").

wall:魏河西长城.note: Built by Wei along the east bank of the Luo River against Qin, from Huayin in the south to Shang Commandery in the north. Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").

wall:齐长城.mod: Pingyin – Mount Tai – Mount Yi – Huangdao, Qingdao, Shandong
wall:齐长城.note: One of the earliest surviving long walls, running from Pingyin (Fangmen) in the west along the Tai–Yi uplands east to Langya and the sea, more than six hundred li long, against Lu, Chu and Yue. Abandoned after the Qin unification (c. 215 BC; Jieshi inscription: "pulled down city walls … levelled strongholds").
